h1: In-store sampling of packaged beer and what it achieves
title: In-Store Sampling of Packaged Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What in-store sampling of packaged beer really buys a brewery, what it costs per sip and where Indian rules allow it.
teaser: A 50 ml sip can sell a six-pack. It can also cost you a day of a salesperson for four bottles sold.
standfirst: Sampling is the oldest trick for moving packaged beer off a shelf. It works when the drinker can buy the beer within reach of the sample. We look at the numbers, the rules and the cases where the money is better spent elsewhere.
sections: Sampling turns a label into a taste

A drinker standing in front of a fridge of 40 unfamiliar labels picks the one they know. That is the whole problem a new packaged beer faces. Sampling cuts through it: a small pour of 30 to 50 ml lets someone taste the beer before they spend ₹200 or more on a can they might not like.

What it buys you is trial. A drinker who has tasted your wheat beer and liked it is far more likely to pick it up next time without help. What it does not buy is loyalty on its own. If the beer is warm on the shelf, out of stock the following week or priced well above the beer next to it, the sample was a one-off gift.
Check the licence before you plan anything

This is where India differs from the brewery guides written for the US or UK. In most states an off licence shop sells sealed bottles for consumption elsewhere. Drinking on the premises is usually not allowed, which rules out a classic in-store tasting table in many shops.

Rules vary by state and change, so treat this as a process, not a verdict:

  • Read the shop's licence conditions and the current state excise notification.
  • Ask the shop owner whether they have run tastings before and under what permission.
  • Where a store cannot host, look at licensed places nearby: a bar with an attached retail counter, a premium store with an on-premise licence, a food festival with a temporary licence.

Never pour without written permission. A notice to the shop costs them far more than your sample ever earned you. Our guide to craft beer rules by state is a sensible starting point before you ask a licensing consultant.
Work out the cost per sample before the cost per day

Sampling looks cheap because the beer is cheap to you. The real cost is people and time. Here is the working for a single four hour session, with round numbers you should replace with your own:

  • Beer: a 330 ml can gives six or seven 50 ml pours. Two cases of 24 cans gives roughly 300 samples. At a cost of ₹60 a can to you, that is ₹2,880.
  • Staff: one person for a half day plus travel, say ₹1,500.
  • Cups, ice box, napkins and a printed price card: about ₹500.

Total, about ₹4,900 for perhaps 150 people actually tasting. If 15 of them buy a four-pack there and then, each sale cost you around ₹325 in sampling spend. That is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to know the number and compare it with a shelf talker, a tap takeover or a staff training session at the shop.
The shop staff matter more than the drinker

The person behind the counter recommends beer all week. You are there for four hours. The best sampling sessions we see spend a third of the time pouring for the staff, explaining the beer in one sentence they can repeat and leaving a simple card that says what it tastes like and what to eat with it.

A store clerk who can say "this one is a light, citrusy wheat beer, good with biryani" will sell more of it on a Tuesday than you sold on Saturday. Treat the session as staff training with drinkers present.

Leave them a can or two of their own to take home where the rules allow it. Someone who has drunk a full serve at leisure explains it far better than someone who had one sip between customers.
Pick the beer and the moment with care

Sample the beer most likely to convert, not your most ambitious one. A 9% imperial stout in a 50 ml cup tastes intense and rarely sells a four-pack in an Indian summer. A clean lager, a wheat beer or a session IPA usually does better with drinkers who are new to craft.

Timing counts. Friday evening and weekend afternoons bring buyers. Weekday mornings bring browsers. Keep the beer between 4 and 7 °C in an insulated box with ice packs: a sample poured at 30 °C ambient tastes flabby and sweet, which is the opposite of what you want a first sip to say. That one detail spoils more sessions than anything else.

Agree a baseline with the shop: how many units of your beer they sold in the four weeks before. Then track the same number for four weeks after. A spike on the day followed by nothing means you bought a crowd, not customers.

Log each session in a sheet with the date, store, beer, samples poured, units sold on the day and units sold in the following month. After ten sessions the pattern is usually obvious: some stores convert and some do not. Putting that kind of evidence behind a sales budget is the part founders find hardest. It is also where a structured look at pricing and route to market pays off.

Your first step: before booking any session, ask one store for its last month of sales for your beer and write it down. Without that baseline, no sampling day can tell you anything.
faqs: Is in-store beer sampling legal in India?
It depends on the state and on the shop's licence. Many off licence shops cannot allow drinking on the premises, so check the current state excise rules and get written permission before pouring.
How big should a beer sample be?
Thirty to 50 ml is the usual range. It is enough to taste the beer and small enough to keep costs and intake low.
Which beer should a brewery sample first?
Usually the most approachable beer in the range, such as a lager or wheat beer, served cold. Strong or very bitter beers convert fewer first-time drinkers.
How do I know if sampling worked?
Compare the store's unit sales of your beer for four weeks before and four weeks after the session, not only the sales on the day.
